Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- A man at the center of a mysterious case of exposure to the deadly biological agent ricin has been arrested, FBI spokesman Richard Kolko said Wednesday. Ricin was found in a room in this Las Vegas, Nevada, extended-stay hotel in February, police say. Roger Bergendorff was taken into custody Wednesday morning in Las Vegas, Nevada, Kolko said. Bergendorff, 57, was hospitalized with what was diagnosed as ricin exposure after the agent was discovered in his hotel room off the Las Vegas Strip. Tests conducted by the FBI determined that the substance contained 2.9 percent active ricin. Its preparation was characterized as "crude," according to the U.S. attorney's office in Las Vegas. According to a press release from the Department of Justice office, a search of Bergendorff's hotel room turned up "an 'Anarchist's Cookbook,' a collection of instructions on poisons and other dangerous recipes, including instructions on the preparation of ricin," two semiautomatic pistols, a rifle and a pistol with a silencer. "FBI searches of Salt Lake City [Utah] storage units rented by Von Bergendorff resulted in the discovery of castor beans, various chemicals used in the production of ricin, a respirator, filters, painter's mask, laboratory glassware, syringes and a notebook on ricin production," the Justice Department release said. Bergendorff is charged with possession of a biological toxin, possession of unregistered firearms and possession of firearms not identified by serial number, according to the U.S. attorney's office. If convicted of all charges, he would face a maximum penalty of 30 years in prison and a fine of $750,000. Bergendorff is scheduled for an initial court appearance at 3 p.m. Wednesday. It is illegal under federal law to possess a biological agent and toxin unless it is used for bona fide research or other peaceful purpose, U.S. Attorney Gregory Bower said in a written statement. Bergendorff's cousin, Thomas Tholen of Riverton, Utah, was indicted by a federal grand jury in Salt Lake City this month, accused of failing to report production and possession of ricin. Ricin is a poison that can be made from the waste of castor bean processing, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It can come in the form of a mist or pellet and can be dissolved in water or weak acid, the agency said. Bergendorff was hospitalized February 14 in Las Vegas after he complained of difficulty breathing. He slipped into a coma and awoke March 14. Bergendorff, 57, is an artist who neighbors said had lived in his cousin's basement before moving to Las Vegas. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Kevin Bohn, Karan Olson and Carol Cratty contributed to this report.

# Suspect Arrested in Ricin Contamination Investigation

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- FBI representative Richard Kolko announced Wednesday that authorities have apprehended the individual connected to a puzzling incident involving exposure to ricin, a lethal biological substance.

Officials report that the toxic agent was discovered back in February inside a room at an extended-stay hotel in Las Vegas, Nevada. Roger Bergendorff was apprehended Wednesday morning in the same city, according to Kolko's statement.

The 57-year-old had been hospitalized after ricin exposure was diagnosed, following the substance's discovery in his hotel accommodation near the Las Vegas Strip. FBI analysis revealed the material contained 2.9 percent active ricin, with the Las Vegas U.S. attorney's office describing its production method as unsophisticated.

A Justice Department statement detailed evidence found during a search of Bergendorff's hotel room, including a copy of "The Anarchist's Cookbook" — a manual containing instructions for creating poisons and other dangerous substances, including ricin preparation methods. Investigators also recovered two semiautomatic handguns, a rifle, and a silencer-equipped pistol from the room.

Additionally, FBI searches of storage facilities in Salt Lake City, Utah, rented under Bergendorff's name yielded castor beans, chemicals associated with ricin manufacturing, protective equipment including a respirator, filters and a painter's mask, laboratory glassware, syringes, and a notebook detailing ricin production methods, per the Justice Department's announcement.

According to prosecutors, Bergendorff now faces charges including possession of a biological toxin, possessing unregistered firearms, and having weapons lacking serial number identification. Should he be convicted on all counts, he could receive up to 30 years of imprisonment along with a $750,000 fine. His initial court hearing was set for 3 p.m. Wednesday.

U.S. Attorney Gregory Bower noted in an official statement that federal regulations prohibit possessing biological toxins unless intended for legitimate research or other peaceful applications.

Separately, Bergendorff's relative, Thomas Tholen from Riverton, Utah, faced indictment earlier this month from a federal grand jury in Salt Lake City for allegedly failing to disclose the manufacturing and possession of ricin.

Per information from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, ricin represents a toxin derivable from castor bean processing byproducts. The substance can exist as mist or pellet form and dissolves readily in water or dilute acid solutions.

Bergendorff's hospitalization began on February 14 following complaints of breathing difficulties, after which he fell into a coma that lasted until he regained consciousness on March 14. Neighbors identified the 57-year-old as an artist who had reportedly resided in his cousin's basement prior to relocating to Las Vegas.

*E-mail to a friend.*

*CNN's Kevin Bohn, Karan Olson and Carol Cratty contributed to this report.*

# Ricin Exposure Investigation Leads to Arrest of Las Vegas Man

Roger Bergendorff, 57, was arrested in Las Vegas, Nevada, in connection with a mysterious ricin exposure case that first came to authorities' attention in February. The arrest marks a significant development in a months-long investigation into how the deadly toxin came to be found in his possession.

## Laboratory Confirms Presence of Toxin

FBI forensic testing confirmed that the substance discovered in Bergendorff's extended-stay hotel room contained 2.9 percent active ricin. Investigators described the preparation as "crude," suggesting the toxin had been produced using rudimentary methods rather than sophisticated laboratory techniques. Ricin, derived from castor beans, is highly toxic even in small quantities and has no known antidote, making its discovery a serious matter for federal investigators.

## Evidence Uncovered in Searches

Subsequent searches conducted at Bergendorff's hotel room, as well as storage units he maintained in Salt Lake City, yielded a disturbing collection of items. Among the evidence recovered were:

- A copy of the "Anarchist's Cookbook," a controversial publication known for containing instructions on producing weapons and explosives
- Multiple firearms
- Castor beans, the raw material from which ricin is extracted
- Various chemicals associated with ricin production
- Laboratory equipment consistent with toxin processing

This combination of materials painted a troubling picture for investigators, suggesting deliberate efforts to produce the biological toxin.

## Federal Charges Filed

As a result of the investigation, Bergendorff now faces multiple federal charges, including possession of a biological toxin and possession of unregistered firearms. If convicted on all counts, he could face a maximum penalty of 30 years in federal prison, along with fines totaling up to $750,000.

## Cousin Also Indicted

The investigation has extended beyond Bergendorff alone. His cousin, Thomas Tholen of Riverton, Utah, has also been indicted in connection with the case, indicating that authorities believe additional individuals may have played a role in the events surrounding the ricin exposure. Details regarding the specific nature of Tholen's alleged involvement have not been fully disclosed, but his indictment suggests the investigation encompassed a broader network than initially understood.

The case remains under continued scrutiny as federal prosecutors prepare to build their case against both defendants.

The announcement comes amid growing concerns from lawmakers about the vulnerability of America's digital infrastructure. Several congressional hearings held in Washington over the past year have highlighted gaps in cybersecurity preparedness across both public and private sectors.

Cybersecurity experts have generally welcomed the new initiative, though some caution that additional resources and funding will be necessary for it to achieve meaningful results. The FBI has requested additional budget allocations in the coming fiscal year specifically earmarked for cyber-related investigations and personnel training.

The bureau indicated that more specific details about the initiative's implementation timeline will be released in the coming weeks, as agencies work to establish new protocols and communication channels.
